summary: Defines EAP-AKA', a small revision of the EAP-AKA method with a new key derivation that binds keys to the access network name and uses SHA-256 instead of SHA-1. It also updates RFC 4187. This is an informational document, updated by RFC 9048 and RFC 9678.

eli5.summary: A phone proves who it is to the network using a SIM card. This update makes the secret keys depend on which network is being used and uses a stronger scrambler.

questions: how does eap-aka' differ from eap-aka
what is a bidding down attack in eap
subtitle: A small revision of EAP-AKA that ties the session keys to the access network name and moves to SHA-256.

tldr.problem: EAP-AKA derives its keys without regard to which access network is in use, so a leaked key from one network could be useful for claiming to be another. 3GPP had also defined a new key derivation that EAP-AKA could not carry unambiguously.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-AKA' is a new EAP method (Type 50) that sends the access network name in AT_KDF_INPUT, negotiates the key derivation with AT_KDF, derives keys with CK' and IK' using a SHA-256 based PRF', and adds an AT_BIDDING attribute to EAP-AKA to prevent bidding down.
tldr.outcome: Keys are bound to a particular network name, which limits the effects of compromised access network nodes and keys. This document is Informational and has since been updated by RFC 9048 and RFC 9678.

today: RFC 5448 is an Informational document that updates RFC 4187, and it has itself been updated by RFC 9048 and RFC 9678, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Why EAP-AKA' Exists
sections.content:
RFC 5448 defines EAP-AKA', a small revision of the EAP-AKA method from RFC 4187. What is new is a key derivation function specified by 3GPP that binds the keys derived within the method to the name of the access network. This limits the effects of compromised access network nodes and keys.

The change has to be unambiguous to both sides: it must not be possible to connect old equipment to new equipment and get the key derivation wrong without a proper error message, and it must be secure against bidding down attacks that try to force the weakest mechanism. So the RFC uses a separate EAP method type. EAP-AKA' uses Type code 50, not 23, and a mutually supported method can be negotiated with the standard EAP mechanisms.

Apart from the points below, EAP-AKA' follows EAP-AKA in all respects. The differences are Type 50, the AT_KDF_INPUT attribute, key derivation function negotiation with AT_KDF, a new way to calculate keys, and SHA-256 instead of SHA-1.
sections.eli5: The old system gave out keys that worked anywhere. The new one stamps the network's name on the key so it only works for that network. It is a new version with its own name so nobody mixes up the old and the new.

sections.title: Network Name and Key Derivation Negotiation
sections.content:
The server sends the access network name to the peer in the AT_KDF_INPUT attribute (attribute type 23). It holds a 2-byte actual network name length, then the name as a UTF-8 string, padded with 1, 2 or 3 zero bytes so the whole attribute is a multiple of 4 bytes. The value MUST be non-empty, and the name is built as specified in 3GPP TS 24.302 as colon-separated fields.

The peer MAY compare the name with its own understanding of it, using a field-by-field comparison where extra fields on one side are ignored. This allows, for example, the peer's "FOO" to match the server's "FOO:BAR". On a mismatch, the peer follows a configurable policy: warn and continue, or fail. If it continues, it MUST use the name received in AT_KDF_INPUT.

The AT_KDF attribute (type 24) lets the server name a key derivation function. Value 1 is the default for EAP-AKA', using CK' and IK'. The server MUST send one or more AT_KDF attributes in the challenge, in order of preference. If the peer will not use the first one, it replies with only an AT_KDF holding its chosen alternative, and the server re-sends the challenge with that choice added to the front of the list, so it appears twice. The peer MUST check that only the requested change occurred.
sections.eli5: The network tells the phone its own name, and the phone checks it matches what it can see. They also agree on which recipe to use for making the keys, and the phone can ask for a different recipe if it prefers.

sections.title: Key Generation and SHA-256
sections.content:
For AT_KDF value 1, the master key is MK = PRF'(IK'|CK',"EAP-AKA'"|Identity). The first 1664 bits of its output are split into K_encr (128 bits), K_aut (256 bits), K_re (256 bits), MSK (512 bits) and EMSK (512 bits). CK' and IK' are derived as specified in 3GPP TS 33.402 from CK, IK and the network name taken from AT_KDF_INPUT.

PRF' is the construction IKEv2 uses: T1 = HMAC-SHA-256 (K, S | 0x01), T2 = HMAC-SHA-256 (K, T1 | S | 0x02), and so on, giving as many bits as needed. AT_MAC uses HMAC-SHA-256-128, the first 16 bytes of the HMAC-SHA-256 value, and AT_CHECKCODE becomes a 32-byte SHA-256 value (or 0 bytes).

The server MUST set the Authentication Management Field (AMF) separation bit to 1, and the peer MUST check that it is 1, otherwise authentication fails. On fast re-authentication the network name must not change: the peer SHOULD NOT try it if the name differs, and the server SHOULD fall back to full authentication. Usernames also change: EAP-AKA' MUST use the leading character "6" instead of "0" for IMSI-based permanent usernames.
sections.eli5: The phone and the network mix the secret with the network's name using a stronger blender, then split the result into separate keys for locking, signing and later use.

sections.title: Preventing Bidding Down of EAP-AKA
sections.content:
Negotiating EAP methods is insecure, so a man-in-the-middle could force both sides onto a weaker method than they both support. To prevent this, the RFC updates EAP-AKA with a new AT_BIDDING attribute (type 136). It is included only in EAP-AKA messages, not EAP-AKA' messages, on the assumption that EAP-AKA' is always preferable.

The attribute has a single D bit, set to 1 if the sender supports EAP-AKA', is willing to use it and prefers it over EAP-AKA. The server sends it in the EAP-Request/AKA-Challenge. If the peer sees that both sides could have used and preferred EAP-AKA', it behaves as if AUTN had been incorrect and fails the authentication. A peer that does not support EAP-AKA' ignores the attribute. It is protected by EAP-AKA integrity, so it cannot be silently removed.

Appendix A states that these are the only changes to RFC 4187. The way MK is calculated there is unchanged.
sections.eli5: Without this, a trickster could convince both sides to use the old, weaker lock even though both have the new one. Now the server writes down that it prefers the new one in a way that cannot be erased.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
The RFC assumes SHA-256 is at least as secure as SHA-1 (the SHA-256 assumption). Under it, EAP-AKA' is at least as secure as EAP-AKA for mutual authentication, replay protection, dictionary attack resistance and fast reconnect, and integrity protection is likely better. Confidentiality is exactly the same. Key derivation gives an effective strength of 128 bits or more, and implementations MUST prevent fast reconnect across method types.

Binding the network name gives extra protection against key leakage. Leaked keys are only useful for access with that name, so a malicious access point cannot claim to be network Y with keys stolen from network X, and a roaming partner cannot easily pose as the home network. This does not stop a compromised access point from representing itself, but it limits the attacker's choices and helps identify compromised networks.

The benefit depends on how names are assigned. If names identify only the access technology, stolen keys cannot be used in a different technology but can still be used by other domains or devices with the same technology. EAP-AKA' does not provide channel bindings as defined in RFC 3748 and RFC 5247.
sections.eli5: If a thief steals a key to one building, it will not open any other building. It does not help if the thief gets into that one building, but it limits the damage.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
EAP-AKA' has EAP Type value 50 in the EAP registry under Method Types. EAP-AKA' shares its attribute space with EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA, so no new attribute registry is needed. New non-skippable attribute values were assigned: 23 for AT_KDF_INPUT and 24 for AT_KDF. A new skippable value, 136, was assigned for AT_BIDDING.

IANA also created a namespace for AT_KDF key derivation function values. Value 0 is reserved, value 1 is EAP-AKA' with CK'/IK', and 2-65535 are unassigned, to be allocated by Specification Required.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers was updated so that each new piece has its own number and nobody reuses one by accident.

messages.label: EAP-Response/Identity
messages.note: Includes the user's Network Access Identifier.

messages.label: EAP-Request/AKA'-Challenge
messages.note: AT_RAND, AT_AUTN, AT_KDF, AT_KDF_INPUT, AT_MAC. The network name travels in AT_KDF_INPUT.

messages.label: EAP-Response/AKA'-Challenge
messages.note: AT_RES, AT_MAC. The peer first compares network names and verifies AUTN and MAC.

messages.label: EAP-Success
messages.note: Sent once RES and MAC are both found correct.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the attribute, MUST be set to 1.

fields.name: D
fields.desc: Set to 1 if the sender supports EAP-AKA', is willing to use it and prefers it over EAP-AKA; otherwise zero.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt.
